svg.title: c.1840 Operating Theatre: Pain, Sepsis & Blood Loss Unsolved
svg.desc: Architectural cross-section of an early-Victorian c.1840 operating theatre before anaesthesia and antiseptics: a conscious patient held down on a blood-stained wooden table, a surgeon in an unwashed blood-stiffened frock coat with bare hands and unsterilised bone saw, a blood-soaked sawdust box underneath, and a crowded unwashed student gallery, resulting in ~45–50% post-operative sepsis mortality.
svg.text: EDEXCEL GCSE HISTORY · EARLY VICTORIAN SURGERY (THE THREE BARRIERS)
c.1840 Operating Theatre: Pain, Sepsis & Blood Loss Unsolved
SOOT-STAINED SKYLIGHT (ONLY LIGHT SOURCE — OPERATIONS HELD AT NOON)

g.text: Knives, saws & silk ligatures kept in velvet
cases, wiped on rags, never boiled; shared
Surgeons wore old street frock coats stiff
with dried blood & pus as a badge of
Dozens of students & public spectators stood
coats right over the open surgical wound.

svg.text: THE THREE GREAT BARRIERS OF c.1840 SURGERY: PAIN (SHOCK) · INFECTION (SEPSIS / GANGRENE) · BLOOD LOSS (HAEMORRHAGE)
Because Germ Theory (1861) was unknown, doctors blamed "bad air" (miasma) while carrying deadly bacteria directly into open wounds on hands, knives & coats.
Nearly 1 in 2 amputation patients died of ward gangrene, pyaemia or erysipelas
WHY HOSPITALS WERE NICKNAMED "GATEWAYS TO DEATH":
Operations were last-resort amputations; deep abdominal or chest surgery was
almost impossible when patients thrashed in agony and wounds rotted afterward.
